public_rationale: OpenAI documented hallucinations in GPT-4V before the post, and an independent 2023 study found object hallucinations across several multimodal models. Multimodal training had therefore not eliminated the problem. OpenAI also reported improvements, so the evidence does not support a stronger claim that error rates could not fall.
limitations: These studies do not isolate the causal effect of multimodal training.
The finding concerns persistence in 2023, not the impossibility of future solutions.
It does not independently verify the Julia Child kitchen exchange.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Multimodal training is not making hallucinations go away.

statement.excerpt: As we can see, multimodal training is not magically making hallucinations go away.

from_speaker: not magically making hallucinations go away
our_interpretation: The plain reading is that adding visual training had not eliminated hallucinations in contemporary multimodal models.
The claim does not say that multimodal training offers no improvement or that elimination is forever impossible.
I assess persistence after multimodal training, not its isolated causal effect relative to otherwise identical text-only training.
For the ongoing state of published evaluations, I use January 1–October 21, 2023, the current research reporting year through publication.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous multimodal models exhibit verified hallucinations after training on visual and language inputs.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative contemporary evaluations establish that hallucinations had been eliminated in the relevant multimodal systems, with the alleged failures explained as something else.

Independent experiments found object hallucinations across several vision-language models. This supports persistence beyond the single kitchen anecdote.
